patient.title: Atezolizumab + carboplatin + etoposide
patient.purpose: To control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and time in treatment should be reviewed with you.

agents.name: Atezolizumab
agents.explanation: Atezolizumab is an antibody against PD-L1, a signal that can reduce an immune cell’s activity. Blocking that signal can help immune cells attack cancer. It works differently from chemotherapy. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even when they look like ordinary treatment tiredness or a minor infection. IV and SC formulations use different doses but both carry immune risks.
agents.watch: Report new cough, breathlessness, diarrhoea, rash, severe headache, weakness, thirst, frequent urination or chest symptoms promptly. Effects can appear during treatment or after the final dose.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, skin, heart, muscles or nerves
Some effects require prolonged treatment or lasting hormone replacement

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but also affects healthy tissues such as bone marrow. Kidney function is used to calculate its dose. It is given during the four-cycle induction phase and stops before atezolizumab-only maintenance.
agents.watch: Report fever, shivering, unexpected bruising, bleeding or persistent vomiting. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, itching, chest tightness, breathing changes or pain around the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection, anaemia and bleeding
Allergic reactions; renal function affects dosing

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA damage can then accumulate and stop cell division. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues can also be affected, explaining low blood counts, hair loss and mouth or bowel problems. Oral absorption differs from IV delivery; the prescribed oral dose must not be inferred from the IV dose.
agents.watch: During an infusion, report dizziness, breathing changes, rash or pain at the drip. At home report fever, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea or poor intake. If capsules are prescribed, follow the exact labelled doses and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose rather than replacing it yourself.
risks: Hair loss, mouth soreness, nausea and bowel changes
Infusion reactions or low blood pressure during administration
Possible later treatment-related leukaemia; discuss longer-term risks

phases.label: Induction · up to four cycles
phases.detail: Day 1 all three medicines; etoposide also Days 2–3. A cycle is 21 days. Confirm the exact IV/SC/oral route plan.

phases.label: Maintenance · after induction
phases.detail: Chemotherapy stops. Atezolizumab continues every 21 days while appropriate; there is no fixed total number here. Review benefit, symptoms and supportive prescriptions.

day_groups.title: Day 1: treatment and checks
day_groups.body: The team checks symptoms and blood tests, then gives atezolizumab, carboplatin and etoposide during induction. Atezolizumab may be IV or SC. Tell staff immediately if you feel unwell during treatment.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm whether Days 2–3 mean IV visits or oral etoposide at home, and check the anti-sickness plan.

day_groups.title: Days 2–3: etoposide during induction
day_groups.body: You either attend for etoposide drips or take the separately prescribed etoposide capsules twice daily, according to your confirmed plan. Capsules are taken on an empty stomach. Maintenance does not include etoposide.
day_groups.action: Do not switch between the IV and oral schedules or infer capsule amounts. Contact the team about missed or vomited doses.

day_groups.title: After the chemotherapy days
day_groups.body: Sickness, reduced appetite, fatigue or bowel changes may occur. Take the anti-sickness medicines on your written schedule, including later days. The team should check coverage after the last chemotherapy day.
day_groups.action: Ask for advice if vomiting continues or you cannot drink. Report new diarrhoea promptly because immune bowel inflammation is also possible.

day_groups.title: Keep checking how you feel
day_groups.body: Blood counts may fall between visits. The day number does not tell you whether your counts are safe. Hair loss, mouth soreness or fatigue can affect daily life; ask for symptom support.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan for fever, shivers or sudden illness, including when your temperature is normal.

day_groups.title: Prepare for the next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle while others persist or appear for the first time. The next dose depends on your review and tests. Around the end of induction, the team discusses whether to move to atezolizumab-only maintenance.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and medicines list. Confirm the next date and which phase and routes are planned.

support.title: Day 1 carboplatin anti-sickness plan
support.text: Carboplatin has a high sickness risk. Your prescription usually includes several anti-sickness medicines with some doses on later days. Follow the written plan even if you initially feel well; contact the team if it is not effective.

support.title: Days 2–3 etoposide and the days afterwards
support.text: The team should account for each chemotherapy day and for two days after the last dose. The later-day plan may overlap the medicines already started on Day 1, so obtain one clear schedule and do not add duplicate doses. Confirm the plan for oral etoposide separately.

support.title: Maintenance support changes
support.text: When only atezolizumab remains, routine chemotherapy anti-sickness steroids and other prophylaxis are not automatically continued. Keep any individual rescue or hormone-replacement plan and the immunotherapy alert card. Do not stop prescribed long-term steroids yourself.

questions.q: What is treatment trying to achieve?
questions.a: Ask how likely this plan is to help control your cancer and symptoms, what alternatives exist, and when you will review benefit.

questions.q: Which routes am I receiving?
questions.a: Confirm IV or SC atezolizumab and IV etoposide on Days 1–3 versus IV Day 1 with oral etoposide twice daily Days 2–3. Ask for a written plan.

questions.q: How long will induction take?
questions.a: Four 21-day cycles occupy about 12 weeks if there are no delays. Chemotherapy then stops; atezolizumab maintenance may continue while appropriate.

questions.q: Who arranges my tests and scans?
questions.a: Confirm blood tests before each cycle, thyroid checks every 3–6 weeks and the consultant’s scan plan. Ask who checks and explains the results.

questions.q: What changes when maintenance starts?
questions.a: Carboplatin and etoposide stop. The visit pattern and anti-sickness plan change, but immune symptom reporting and blood/hormone checks continue.

questions.q: Who do I call outside clinic hours?
questions.a: Keep your oncology emergency number and written temperature/symptom instructions. Do not wait for the next appointment when unwell; show your immunotherapy alert card.

chapters.title: Understanding this treatment
chapters.intro: A three-medicine induction phase, then atezolizumab-only maintenance.

items.title: Your treatment aim
items.text: To control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and time in treatment should be reviewed with you.

items.title: How the phases fit together
items.text: Induction: atezolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1, with etoposide on Days 1–3, repeated every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: carboplatin and etoposide stop; atezolizumab alone continues every 21 days while appropriate. The fourth cycle ends about 12 weeks after starting if there are no delays; maintenance has no fixed total duration in this regimen.

items.title: Confirm your route plan
items.text: Confirm your written route plan. Atezolizumab may be a drip (IV) or an injection under the skin of the thigh (SC). Etoposide may be IV on Days 1–3, or IV on Day 1 with prescribed capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. These schedules use different doses; do not change route or convert doses yourself. A separately prescribed four-week IV atezolizumab maintenance plan uses NCCP 00593 and is outside this 21-day calendar.

items.title: Reviewing benefit and choices
items.text: Symptoms, scans and how treatment affects your daily life all matter. Ask when benefit will be reviewed and what would prompt a delay, change or stop. There is no universal scan calendar in this NCCP regimen. You can revisit consent and discuss supportive care at any point.

chapters.title: Before the first treatment
chapters.intro: Use this as a conversation checklist. Your own hospital’s instructions and prescription take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe your usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin symptoms and ability to manage daily tasks. Mention autoimmune illness, organ transplant, previous lung inflammation, infections and all regular medicines. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you. Do not minimise symptoms because you are worried treatment will be delayed.

items.title: Make the first week manageable
items.text: Have the oncology and out-of-hours numbers available, a working thermometer, your medicine schedule and a way to get urgent help. Ask who to ring if you miss a supportive medicine. Plan transport and practical help if needed. Bring your questions and, if you wish, someone you trust to listen and take notes.

items.title: During the infusion visit
items.text: Expect symptom and blood-test review before medicines are released. Chemotherapy is given through agreed venous access; atezolizumab may be a drip or a thigh injection. Tell staff immediately about pain or swelling around the treatment site, itching, flushing, dizziness or breathing changes. Preparation and observation add to the visit time.

chapters.title: What your tests and scans are checking
chapters.intro: Different checks answer different questions: whether treatment is safe today, whether a symptom needs investigation, and whether the cancer is responding.

items.title: Blood counts: three separate jobs
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection; a low level can make infection dangerous. Haemoglobin carries oxygen; a low level can contribute to tiredness and breathlessness. Platelets help stop bleeding; low levels can cause bruising or bleeding. Feeling well does not prove your counts are normal, and a previous normal result does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Kidney, liver and hormone checks
items.text: Kidney function helps the team calculate carboplatin and review etoposide dosing. Liver and kidney tests can also reveal immune inflammation or other problems before symptoms develop. Glucose is checked each cycle and thyroid function every three to six weeks. Fatigue, weakness, thirst, dizziness or new headaches may need extra tests; do not assume that they are ordinary treatment effects.

items.title: Scans and the treatment decision
items.text: Your team sets the scan schedule and compares scans with symptoms and examination findings. Stable disease can be a worthwhile result. New symptoms need review even before the next scan. An unusual scan pattern sometimes needs clarification; do not assume that apparent growth is simply an immune response or that feeling worse means treatment is working.

items.title: Why a delay or a change can be appropriate
items.text: A pause may allow recovery or investigation. Chemotherapy doses can sometimes be reduced. Atezolizumab is generally held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which drug is changing and why; stopping one drug does not automatically mean stopping every part of the plan. Long-term treatment decisions belong in a discussion about benefit, risk and what matters to you.

chapters.title: Side effects: what they mean and what to do
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet. You do not need to work out the cause before asking for help.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite change
items.text: Medicines can stimulate sickness pathways in the gut and brain. Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed, even when you initially feel well. Smaller meals and frequent sips may be easier. Report poor control early so the plan can be adjusted. Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Do not wait until you are very dehydrated.

items.title: Fatigue: common, but not always “just treatment”
items.text: Fatigue may reflect treatment, disturbed sleep, reduced intake, anaemia or another illness. Balance rest with manageable movement and prioritise activities that matter to you. A sudden change, severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment; hormone problems and other complications can resemble ordinary tiredness. Tell the team how fatigue affects daily life, not just that you feel tired.

items.title: Mouth soreness, ulcers and taste
items.text: Treatment can injure the lining of the mouth. Use a soft toothbrush, gentle mouth care and the rinses recommended by your team. Choose softer foods and avoid foods that sting. Ask for pain relief early. Report ulcers, white patches, painful swallowing or reduced intake; difficulty drinking or fever needs urgent advice. Arrange dental care with the oncology team before procedures.

items.title: Diarrhoea or abdominal pain
items.text: Chemotherapy can upset the bowel, and atezolizumab can cause bowel inflammation. Report new diarrhoea promptly, including stools above your usual pattern, blood, mucus, pain or night-time symptoms. Do not assume that it is ordinary chemotherapy upset. Severe pain, bleeding or dehydration needs urgent assessment.

items.title: Constipation
items.text: Anti-sickness drugs, opioid painkillers, less food and less movement can slow the bowel. Ask about a bowel plan if you are prone to constipation or take opioids. Keep track of your usual pattern. Increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass wind needs prompt assessment rather than simply increasing laxatives.

items.title: Bruising, bleeding or breathlessness
items.text: Chemotherapy may reduce platelets or red cells. Report unexpected bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding gums or increasing breathlessness. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness, severe chest pain or severe breathing difficulty need emergency help. Do not start iron or alter blood thinners without review: the cause and treatment need to be established.

items.title: Skin, hair and nerve changes
items.text: Etoposide can cause hair loss, which may affect scalp and body hair. Ask about practical support before it begins. Report a new or spreading rash, tingling, numbness or weakness. Blisters, peeling skin or sores involving eyes or mouth need urgent assessment because immune skin reactions can be serious. Use gentle skin care and ask about suitable sun protection.

chapters.title: Atezolizumab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received atezolizumab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Treatment may harm a developing baby; ask for a written contraception plan covering all three medicines and the period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment; confirm when it would be safe to restart. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Ask about barrier protection and handling body fluids under your hospital’s advice.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

chapters.title: Your route and capsule plan
chapters.intro: The NCCP source lists four combinations of routes. Your team must select and prescribe one clearly.

items.title: IV or SC atezolizumab
items.text: The IV formulation runs through a drip; the SC formulation is injected under the skin of the thigh. Their doses differ. The nurse checks the correct formulation and injection site. Both can cause immune and administration reactions; tell staff about pain, swelling, rash, dizziness or breathing changes.

items.title: Etoposide Days 2–3
items.text: The standard IV schedule has a drip on all three days. The oral alternative has IV etoposide on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. Follow the exact capsule label and empty-stomach instructions. Do not calculate a replacement oral dose from a drip dose, split a capsule or double a missed dose. Ask the team what to do after a missed or vomited dose.

items.title: Handling and supply
items.text: Keep capsules in their original labelled packaging, away from children. Follow the pharmacy’s handling and disposal advice; ask what carers should do if a capsule is damaged. Check the full supply and both daily doses before leaving the unit. Do not use remaining capsules for a later cycle unless the team confirms the new prescription.

items.title: Changing phase
items.text: All carboplatin and etoposide finish when induction ends. Atezolizumab-only maintenance in this guide is every three weeks. If your team selects four-week IV maintenance, obtain the separate written schedule; this guide must not be used to convert it.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: In a randomised trial in previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, adding atezolizumab to carboplatin and IV etoposide improved survival and delayed progression on average. This cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.interpretation: In a randomised trial in previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, adding atezolizumab to carboplatin and IV etoposide improved survival and delayed progression on average. This cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.population: Adults with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in IMpower133.
evidence.limitations: IMpower133 studied IV atezolizumab with IV etoposide. It did not directly randomise the SC formulation or the Day 2–3 oral etoposide alternative; those are separate NCCP-listed schedules. Trial averages are not an individual prognosis or a comparison with another immunotherapy.

sections.title: Appointments and time in the unit
sections.text: Day 1 order: atezolizumab, carboplatin, then etoposide. Atezolizumab IV first infusion is 60 minutes, later 30 minutes if tolerated; SC injection takes about 7 minutes. Carboplatin infusion is 30 minutes and etoposide IV is 60 minutes. Total unit time also includes checks, preparation and observation. sections.title: Your written formulation plan
sections.text: Confirm your written route plan. Atezolizumab may be a drip (IV) or an injection under the skin of the thigh (SC). Etoposide may be IV on Days 1–3, or IV on Day 1 with prescribed capsules twice daily on Days 2–3. These schedules use different doses; do not change route or convert doses yourself. A separately prescribed four-week IV atezolizumab maintenance plan uses NCCP 00593 and is outside this 21-day calendar.

sections.title: Travel, support and medicines
sections.text: Induction usually involves treatment on three consecutive days or one IV day plus prescribed capsules at home. Ask about transport, work, caring responsibilities and who to call about capsules or symptoms. Carry the immunotherapy alert card.

sections.title: Tests and maintenance
sections.text: FBC, liver, renal and glucose profile before every cycle; thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks. Scans and other disease assessment follow the consultant plan. Continue symptom review during maintenance and after atezolizumab stops because immune effects may be delayed. Confirm which team books each test and who reviews it before treatment.

chronology_notes.title: About 12 weeks of induction if on schedule
chronology_notes.text: Four 21-day cycles include both treatment days and the interval before the next cycle; delays can extend the course.

chronology_notes.title: No fixed total maintenance length
chronology_notes.text: Atezolizumab continues while the team judges it appropriate, until progression or unacceptable toxicity under this NCCP regimen. The plan is reviewed with you.

chronology_notes.title: Day 2–3 route matters
chronology_notes.text: These days are IV visits or prescribed oral etoposide twice daily. They are not days without treatment during induction.

chronology_notes.title: Checks continue after chemotherapy
chronology_notes.text: Maintenance still requires cycle bloods, thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks and ongoing symptom review. Immune effects may begin after the last atezolizumab dose.

patient.title: Serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide
patient.purpose: This treatment aims to control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and daily life is individual; it is generally not offered with an expectation of cure.

agents.name: Serplulimab
agents.explanation: Serplulimab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Some cancers use PD-L1 or PD-L2 to engage this switch and reduce the immune response. Blocking it can help immune cells attack cancer. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin and hormone glands
Immune effects can also involve the heart, pancreas, nervous system or blood cells
Some hormone effects need lasting replacement treatment; immune effects can begin after the final dose

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 5 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 5 mg.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, nausea and vomiting can occur. An allergic reaction is also possible: tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, itchy, tight-chested or unwell during the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection or bleeding

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.alias: Chemotherapy; IV or a separately prescribed capsule alternative
agents.mechanism: Interferes with DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide blocks topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps untangle DNA. It can leave DNA breaks unrepaired so that dividing cancer cells die. Healthy dividing cells are affected too, which can lower blood counts, irritate the mouth and bowel and cause hair loss. Kidney function, liver tests and albumin help the team choose a safe dose. Capsules have different dosing instructions from the drip.
agents.watch: Report fever or sudden illness immediately. During a drip, tell the nurse about dizziness, flushing, breathing difficulty or pain at the cannula. If capsules are prescribed, do not take an extra dose after vomiting or a missed dose without advice.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hair loss and mouth or bowel symptoms
Infusion reactions and low blood pressure
A delayed risk of treatment-related leukaemia

phases.detail: After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen.

day_groups.body: Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed. day_groups.title: Prepare for your next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle; others can continue or appear for the first time. Improvement does not prove your blood counts have recovered. The next treatment depends on your review and tests.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and questions. Confirm the next appointment: the next Day 1 is usually 21 days after this cycle's Day 1, if treatment proceeds.

support.title: Induction: plan each treatment day
support.text: Day 1 carboplatin has a stronger anti-sickness plan. Days 2–3 etoposide also need planned cover, with review for two days after the final chemotherapy dose. Ask for one reconciled schedule; do not add another steroid or anti-sickness course yourself.

support.title: Maintenance: a different prescription
support.text: Serplulimab alone usually does not need the routine chemotherapy anti-sickness course. Continue the alert card and immune symptom checks; new nausea or vomiting may need investigation, not just extra anti-sickness tablets.

questions.q: How will we know if it is helping?
questions.a: Ask your oncologist what the treatment is aiming to achieve for you, when scans are planned and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping it. How you feel and the amount of side effects do not reliably show how well treatment is working.

questions.q: Why might a cycle be delayed?
questions.a: A delay can give time to recover or investigate a new symptom. It is a safety decision, not a personal failure. Ask which medicines are affected, what needs to improve and when you will be reviewed.

questions.q: Will I get every side effect?
questions.a: No. The body map shows selected possibilities, not a prediction. Ask about common effects, serious less common effects, and any long-term risks that matter particularly to you. The same symptom can have several causes.

questions.q: What should I organise before starting?
questions.a: Confirm blood-test and Day Ward arrangements, transport home, your medicines schedule and a thermometer. Keep the oncology contact instructions and immunotherapy alert card available. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information if useful.

questions.q: What else belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: Your priorities, expected benefit, alternatives including supportive care, fertility, contraception, pregnancy or breastfeeding, work, driving and the possibility of lasting side effects. You can ask more questions or reconsider treatment at any stage.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean the treatment is working better?
questions.a: No. Side effects are not a reliable personal measure of cancer response. Report them so they can be treated; do not tolerate serious symptoms in the hope that they are a sign of benefit.

questions.q: Do all three medicines continue indefinitely?
questions.a: Induction lasts four planned 21-day cycles unless treatment needs to stop earlier. On Day 1 you receive serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide by drip. With the standard IV schedule, etoposide is repeated on Days 2 and 3. After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen.

questions.q: What should I say when calling about a symptom?
questions.a: Give the current medicines or say you are in maintenance, the last treatment date, what changed and when, your temperature and whether you can eat, drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect every detail.

questions.q: Which checks continue afterwards?
questions.a: Immune effects can arise after the final serplulimab dose. Keep the alert card and urgent contact plan. Follow-up of blood counts, organ changes and scans follows the team’s plan; no universal scan interval is imposed by this regimen.

questions.q: Will I come to hospital on all three treatment days?
questions.a: Usually with the standard IV induction plan, yes. Some people receive a separate capsule prescription for Days 2 and 3. Confirm the route and exact schedule before arranging transport; never substitute capsules for a drip yourself.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit an etoposide capsule dose?
questions.a: Contact the oncology team or pharmacist for instructions. Do not double the next dose or repeat a vomited dose without advice. Store and handle capsules exactly as the pharmacy advises.

chapters.title: Understanding the treatment aim
chapters.intro: Take one section at a time and discuss what matters to you.

items.title: What do the words mean?
items.text: Small-cell describes the cancer cells seen under the microscope. Extensive-stage means it is too widespread for the limited-stage treatment approach. First-line means the first drug treatment for this stage. This regimen combines two chemotherapy medicines with serplulimab immunotherapy.

items.title: What is treatment trying to achieve?
items.text: The usual aims are cancer control, symptom relief and longer life while considering quality of life. It is generally not given with an expectation of cure. Some people have a prolonged response; others do not. Your team uses your cancer tests, general health and preferences to choose a plan.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask about other appropriate systemic treatments, a clinical trial and symptom-focused care. Palliative care can support symptoms and daily life while you receive active cancer treatment. This regimen has no required PD-L1 cutoff; that does not guarantee benefit.

chapters.title: Before the first infusion
chapters.intro: Your hospital’s instructions take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin and nerve symptoms. Mention autoimmune illness, previous lung inflammation, infection and all medicines including steroids and supplements. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you.

items.title: Prepare the practical details
items.text: Keep the oncology and out-of-hours numbers, a thermometer and the immunotherapy alert card available. Check blood-test appointments, transport and who can help at home. Ask for written medicine directions and accessible information.

items.title: What happens on the day?
items.text: Serplulimab is given first over about 60 minutes at the first visit. If tolerated, later doses may take about 30 minutes. Carboplatin takes about 30 minutes and IV etoposide about 60 minutes. Assessment, preparation and observation add time. Days 2–3 need further etoposide visits unless the separate oral alternative has been prescribed. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, itching, chest pain, dizziness, breathing changes or pain around the drip.

chapters.title: Etoposide: confirm the route
chapters.intro: There are two NCCP schedules. Your prescription chooses one.

items.title: Standard IV schedule
items.text: Etoposide is given by drip on each of Days 1, 2 and 3 during induction. Serplulimab and carboplatin are given on Day 1. The next cycle is planned 21 days after Day 1, if your team confirms it.

items.title: Separate IV and capsule alternative
items.text: Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed. Capsules are supplied in different strengths; your label specifies the number to take. Do not open, crush or share capsules. Ask the pharmacist about handling, storage and returning unused doses.

chapters.title: What tests and scans check
chapters.intro: A normal earlier test does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection, platelets help stop bleeding, and red cells carry oxygen. Counts can fall between visits. You cannot know a count from the day of the cycle or from feeling well.

items.title: Kidneys, liver and hormones
items.text: Kidney function helps set carboplatin dosing and may affect etoposide dosing. Liver tests and albumin also matter for etoposide. Serplulimab can inflame organs and hormone glands, so blood glucose and thyroid checks continue during maintenance. Report new symptoms even if an earlier test was normal.

items.title: Scans and treatment review
items.text: The team sets the scan schedule and reviews scans with symptoms and examination. Stable cancer can be a worthwhile result. Report new symptoms before the next scan; do not assume worsening is evidence that immune treatment is working.

items.title: Delays and changed doses
items.text: Chemotherapy may be delayed or reduced for toxicity. Serplulimab is held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which medicine is changing and why. Omitted checks are not the same as normal results.

chapters.title: Side effects and what to do
chapters.intro: Selected possibilities are shown; this is not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite
items.text: Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines as directed. Small meals and regular sips may help. Report poor control early; persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine needs prompt advice.

items.title: Fatigue and weakness
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Sudden severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment: infection, anaemia or hormone problems can resemble ordinary tiredness.

items.title: Mouth and bowels
items.text: Use gentle mouth care and report painful ulcers or difficulty drinking. Report new diarrhoea, abdominal pain or blood in stools promptly because immune bowel inflammation is possible. Ask about constipation from anti-sickness drugs or pain medicines; severe pain, swelling or vomiting needs assessment.

items.title: Hair, skin, hearing and nerves
items.text: Chemotherapy can cause hair loss. Report new hearing changes, numbness or weakness, and tell the team if these affect balance or daily tasks. Serplulimab can cause immune skin reactions: blistering, peeling or sores around the eyes or mouth need urgent advice.

items.title: Bruising and bleeding
items.text: Report unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness or severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Do not change prescribed blood thinners without advice.

chapters.title: Serplulimab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received serplulimab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

items.title: Muscle weakness and vision changes
items.text: New muscle weakness, tiring much more easily, drooping eyelids, swallowing difficulty or new visual symptoms need urgent advice. Difficulty breathing or swallowing needs emergency care. Serplulimab can cause serious nerve-muscle or eye inflammation; do not wait for the next appointment.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before starting if relevant. Do not become pregnant or breastfeed during this treatment. NCCP specifies effective contraception during serplulimab and for at least six months after the last dose for women of childbearing potential; the team must reconcile all medicines into one written contraception and breastfeeding plan. Report a possible pregnancy promptly.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: A randomised study found that adding serplulimab to carboplatin and etoposide helped people with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer live longer than chemotherapy alone.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups. They cannot predict your own response or length of life. Ask what benefit is realistic for you and what matters most in your daily life.
evidence.population: Adults with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in ASTRUM-005.
evidence.limitations: The trial studied selected people with performance status 0–1 and IV etoposide. The NCCP regimen permits performance status 0–2 and an oral alternative, so the trial is not a separate result for every NCCP-eligible person or for the oral schedule.

drug_mechanisms.serplulimab: Serplulimab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Some cancers use PD-L1 or PD-L2 to engage this switch and reduce the immune response. Blocking it can help immune cells attack cancer. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even after treatment stops.
drug_mechanisms.etoposide: Etoposide blocks topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps untangle DNA. It can leave DNA breaks unrepaired so that dividing cancer cells die. Healthy dividing cells are affected too, which can lower blood counts, irritate the mouth and bowel and cause hair loss. Kidney function, liver tests and albumin help the team choose a safe dose. Capsules have different dosing instructions from the drip.

evidence.applicability: Direct first-line ES-SCLC evidence for the IV combination, with narrower performance-status eligibility than NCCP and no head-to-head immunotherapy comparison.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing; normal tissues can also be affected. Carboplatin dosing is tailored using a verified kidney-function result; low blood counts can be an important limiting effect.
agents.watch: Report changes in urine, hearing, ringing in the ears, numbness or daily function. Tell the team about infection, unusual bruising or bleeding and any symptoms during the infusion.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA breaks can remain unrepaired and cancer cells may stop dividing or die. Healthy cells are also affected; the infusion or prescribed capsules deliver the same medicine by different routes.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, mouth sores or diarrhoea. Tell the nurse about faintness, rash or breathing difficulty during an infusion. If capsules are prescribed, use the exact pharmacy instructions and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding

questions.q: Why are there three treatment days?
questions.a: Etoposide is planned on three consecutive days. Usually you attend for infusions on all three. The alternative capsule plan is only used when prescribed and clearly labelled by your team.

questions.q: Are etoposide capsules the same dose as the drip?
questions.a: No. The source oral alternative has a different dose and twice-daily schedule. Your prescription and pharmacy label specify your individual dose and capsule strengths. Do not convert it yourself.

questions.q: Will I have radiotherapy or immunotherapy too?
questions.a: This guide covers Carboplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

questions.q: How long does the course last?
questions.a: The source describes 4–6 cycles every 21 days, or stopping for cancer progression or unacceptable side effects. Your team confirms the intended course and may change it earlier. The passport pages are reusable records, not a prescription for a fixed number of visits.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be assessed and treated; your team reviews benefit with the agreed clinical and scan plan.

questions.q: Why might treatment be delayed or changed?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney/liver function or symptoms may need time to recover. A dose may change to reduce lasting harm. Ask which medicine changes, why, and when it will be reviewed.

questions.q: What should I say when I call?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment day, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect information.

questions.q: Can this guide decide whether treatment is safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions need your clinical results, symptoms, previous toxicity and prescriber/pharmacy review. This guide helps you understand and discuss the plan.

items.title: Why two medicines?
items.text: The platinum drug damages DNA and etoposide interferes with DNA repair. Using them together attacks cell growth in different ways. Healthy cells can also be affected.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

items.title: Days 2 and 3
items.text: Continue etoposide by the prescribed route, with risk-appropriate anti-sickness prevention each treatment day.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines may lower blood counts. Infection can become serious quickly; follow the urgent advice plan for fever, chills or sudden illness.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Platinum medicines may affect hearing, nerves and kidneys, and some changes can last. Tell the team promptly about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or reduced urine.

items.title: Mouth, bowel, hair and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness, nausea, bowel changes, hair loss and tiredness can affect daily life. Ask for help with symptoms; call urgently if you cannot drink or symptoms are severe.

items.title: Later effects
items.text: Etoposide can be associated with a later blood cancer. Discuss serious and lasting risks together with likely benefit and alternatives.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA breaks can remain unrepaired and cancer cells may stop dividing or die. agents.name: Cisplatin

questions.q: Why are there three treatment days?
questions.a: Etoposide is planned on three consecutive days. Usually you attend for infusions on all three. The alternative capsule plan is only used when prescribed and clearly labelled by your team.

questions.q: Are etoposide capsules the same dose as the drip?
questions.a: No. The source oral alternative has a different dose and twice-daily schedule. Your prescription and pharmacy label specify your individual dose and capsule strengths. Do not convert it yourself.

questions.q: Will I have radiotherapy or immunotherapy too?
questions.a: This guide covers Cisplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

questions.q: How long does the course last?
questions.a: The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response. The passport pages are reusable records, not a prescription for a fixed number of visits.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be assessed and treated; your team reviews benefit with the agreed clinical and scan plan.

questions.q: Why might treatment be delayed or changed?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney/liver function or symptoms may need time to recover. A dose may change to reduce lasting harm. Ask which medicine changes, why, and when it will be reviewed.

questions.q: What should I say when I call?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment day, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect information.

questions.q: Can this guide decide whether treatment is safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions need your clinical results, symptoms, previous toxicity and prescriber/pharmacy review. This guide helps you understand and discuss the plan.

items.title: Why two medicines?
items.text: The platinum drug damages DNA and etoposide interferes with DNA repair. Using them together attacks cell growth in different ways. Healthy cells can also be affected.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

items.text: Mouth soreness, nausea, bowel changes, hair loss and tiredness can affect daily life. Ask for help with symptoms; call urgently if you cannot drink or symptoms are severe.

patient.title: Carboplatin + Oral Etoposide
patient.purpose: This chemotherapy combination aims to control extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer, ease symptoms and help people live longer. Expected benefit depends on the cancer, general health and treatment choices. Ask what the team hopes it will achieve for you.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. The dose is tailored using kidney function because the kidneys clear carboplatin.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Report infection or unusual bruising/bleeding promptly and describe any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist

agents.name: Oral etoposide
agents.mechanism: Interferes with DNA repair and cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme involved in DNA structure and repair. DNA damage can stop cancer cells dividing. Healthy blood-forming and other cells can also be affected. Absorption by mouth varies, so oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable.
agents.watch: Follow the exact capsule schedule and record doses. Report missed/vomited doses, infection, bruising, mouth ulcers or severe bowel symptoms. Do not double or convert doses yourself.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and mouth soreness

items.title: The treatment aim

items.title: What the evidence can tell us
items.text: The studies cited by NCCP support platinum–etoposide treatment and provide background on using etoposide by mouth, but they did not test this exact carboplatin plus all-oral three-day schedule. The oral comparison used cisplatin and a mixture of intravenous and oral etoposide. A separate pooled analysis compared platinum choices across several trials. These results cannot give a precise survival estimate for this prescription or predict your individual benefit.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Tell the team early so symptoms can be assessed and treated.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines can lower blood counts, increasing infection, bleeding or anaemia risk. Attend monitoring and report sudden illness, bruising or bleeding.

items.title: Mouth, stomach and energy
items.text: Sickness, diarrhoea, constipation, mouth soreness, appetite loss, fatigue and hair loss may occur. Ask for help early; inability to drink or persistent vomiting needs urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Tell the team about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness, balance problems or reduced urine. Some effects can persist after treatment.

items.title: Less common serious effects
items.text: Serious allergic or skin reactions can occur. Etoposide also carries a risk of secondary leukaemia; ask the team to explain serious and lasting risks in your situation.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Call your unit urgently for fever at its stated threshold, shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, unusual or uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Swelling of the tongue/throat or trouble breathing can be an emergency. Report new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty walking promptly.

items.title: What to say when you call
items.text: Give the regimen name, last infusion and capsule dose, symptoms and when they began. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect all the details.

chapters.title: Reviewing the course and next steps

items.title: After a change or stop
items.text: Confirm which medicines stop or continue, how unused capsules are returned, and follow-up for ongoing symptoms. Ask who will contact you about the next treatment or supportive-care plan.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Are oral capsules a weaker form of chemotherapy?
questions.a: No. Etoposide capsules are chemotherapy and can cause serious effects. Their absorption differs from an infusion, so only the treating team can choose or change the dose.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a dose?
questions.a: If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose or extend the course. The manufacturer leaflet advises taking the next dose when due; inform your oncology pharmacist/team and follow your written plan. If you vomit after a dose, contact the team for instructions rather than automatically taking replacement capsules. BC Cancer specifically advises no repeat dose after vomiting within one hour unless the healthcare team directs it. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs urgent advice.

questions.q: Do I continue capsules every day until the next infusion?
questions.a: No. This regimen prescribes twice-daily etoposide on Days 1–3 only. Use your own written calendar and wait for the team to confirm the next cycle.

questions.q: Will I always have a fixed number of cycles?
questions.a: The current NCCP source continues this regimen until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with ongoing review. Your team agrees the number of cycles and may stop or change earlier.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is this the same as pemetrexed with pembrolizumab?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed on its own for maintenance or second-line treatment of selected non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. If pembrolizumab or another immunotherapy is also prescribed, use the matching combination regimen and its additional consent, monitoring and urgent advice. Pemetrexed with pembrolizumab maintenance is a different treatment plan.

questions.q: What is maintenance treatment?
questions.a: Maintenance means continuing cancer treatment after the initial chemotherapy has finished and the cancer has not progressed. In this regimen pemetrexed is the only anti-cancer medicine. Your team confirms whether it is being continued from your earlier combination or started as a new maintenance medicine.

questions.q: How many cycles will I have?
questions.a: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.

questions.q: Can I stop the vitamins when platinum treatment stops?
questions.a: Do not stop them because platinum stops. Folic acid and B12 protect against pemetrexed toxicity and continue according to the pemetrexed plan. The team checks your existing vitamin schedule at a phase change.

questions.q: How long will I be at the unit?
questions.a: Pemetrexed is infused into a vein over about 10 minutes on Day 1. The whole visit is longer because it includes blood-result review, symptom checks, medicines, preparation and observation. The team can use a cannula or suitable existing line; this regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump.

questions.q: Can I take my usual painkillers?
questions.a: Check with the team before using ibuprofen, other anti-inflammatory painkillers, aspirin or any new medicine. Kidney function and the medicine determine whether and when it needs interruption. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask for a written plan.

day_groups.body: Continue folic acid and monitor symptoms. Your B12 injection is due every three cycles and may be booked on a treatment day.

support.title: Folic acid every day
support.text: The source uses folic acid 350–1000 micrograms daily. Take at least five doses in the seven days before the first pemetrexed, continue throughout treatment and for 21 days after the final dose. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

support.title: Vitamin B12 injection
support.text: The source uses vitamin B12 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections may be on treatment day. A change from platinum treatment to maintenance does not automatically restart the B12 clock: your team checks the last dose and the next due date.

support.title: One steroid prescription
support.text: Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. Your pharmacist or prescriber should give one clear steroid schedule that also accounts for any anti-sickness medicines. Do not add a second steroid course yourself.

support.title: Low-risk anti-sickness plan
support.text: Pemetrexed on its own has a low sickness risk. Take the prescribed prevention and rescue medicines and call if sickness persists. A previous platinum anti-sickness course should be reviewed when moving to pemetrexed alone.

support.title: Kidneys and other medicines
support.text: Check with the team before using ibuprofen, other anti-inflammatory painkillers, aspirin or any new medicine. Kidney function and the medicine determine whether and when it needs interruption. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask for a written plan.

support.title: Reporting symptoms and getting help
support.text: Keep your 24-hour oncology number available, record symptoms and ask for practical or emotional support early.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the treatment setting
evidence.intro: Maintenance and second-line studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Selected advanced NSCLC populations after prior chemotherapy; the maintenance trials included patients without progression.
evidence.comparison_label: Placebo/supportive care in maintenance; docetaxel in second-line treatment
evidence.interpretation: Maintenance studies found longer disease control or survival with pemetrexed than placebo in selected patients whose cancer had not progressed after initial chemotherapy. One studied starting pemetrexed after a different chemotherapy combination; another studied continuing it after pemetrexed and cisplatin. A separate second-line study found similar survival to docetaxel with fewer important blood-count side effects. These historical comparisons do not predict an individual outcome or describe pemetrexed plus immunotherapy.

chronology_notes.title: Before the first pemetrexed
chronology_notes.text: Folate preparation and the first B12 injection start before the infusion. When already on pemetrexed, confirm the established vitamin schedule.

chronology_notes.title: Day before each dose
chronology_notes.text: Start the prescribed rash-prevention steroid the day before pemetrexed; the reference cycle starts at infusion Day 1.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment length
chronology_notes.text: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.

chronology_notes.title: After the final dose
chronology_notes.text: Folate continues for 21 days after the last pemetrexed; persistent symptoms and follow-up remain important.

patient.administration_text: Pemetrexed is infused into a vein over about 10 minutes on Day 1. clinical.component_rationale: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
key_points: NCCP00222a maintenance and 00222b second-line are distinct indications; both exclude predominantly squamous NSCLC.
Pemetrexed 500 mg/m² IV over 10 minutes on Day 1 every 21 days until progression or unacceptable toxicity.

Renal clearance <45 mL/min, haemodialysis and severe hepatic impairment are outside the routine pathway.
Grade 2 first neurotoxicity: hold to baseline then 100% pemetrexed; grade ≥3 or any recurrence: discontinue.
Any grade diarrhoea requiring admission triggers the severe pathway; mucositis and other toxicities have different restart percentages.
No fixed cycle cap or automatic immune-specific monitoring belongs to standalone pemetrexed.

rationale.summary: Pemetrexed monotherapy provides a source-listed maintenance or second-line option for selected advanced non-squamous NSCLC. Confirm which treatment context, prior therapy and current alternatives fit the patient.
rationale.setting: Non-squamous NSCLC · standalone maintenance or second-line chemotherapy
rationale.line: Maintenance immediately after platinum chemotherapy without progression, or second-line after prior chemotherapy.
factors: Histology, prior drugs and disease progression status.
Performance status, organ function, toxicity history, patient priorities and current molecular/systemic options.
Vitamin/steroid preparation and medicine-interaction plan.
alternatives: Discuss current disease-specific MDT options, other systemic therapy, trials and supportive care, including not proceeding.
limitations: Maintenance trials selected patients whose disease had not progressed; PARAMOUNT additionally randomised ECOG 0–1 patients after four pemetrexed/cisplatin cycles. NCCP eligibility ECOG 0–2 is broader.
JMEN studied switch maintenance after non-pemetrexed platinum doublets; PARAMOUNT studied continuation. Overall and non-squamous subgroup results and time origins must remain separate.

Hanna2004 enrolled a historical all-histology second-line NSCLC population; its overall survival comparison is not a modern non-squamous subgroup prediction or proof of a pemetrexed survival advantage.
These trials predate modern immunotherapy and many molecular treatments; they do not rank contemporary options or demonstrate pembrolizumab/pemetrexed maintenance benefit.
